h1:
Mae Hong Son in 1 Day
The Old Town
intro: Only have a single day in Mae Hong Son's old town? You can still see the best of it without ever driving out of the city, because almost everything worth doing is clustered around Nong Jong Kham, the lake in the middle of town. This plan walks you from the early Shan market, to the twin lakeside temples, up Doi Kong Mu for a view over the whole valley, and finishes at the night market after dark.
chips: ⛰️ City view from Doi Kong Mu

blocks.html: Mae Hong Son's old town is small and easy to walk. Almost all the main sights ring Nong Jong Kham, the lake at the center of town, just a few hundred metres apart — only Doi Kong Mu needs a ride up the hill. This plan covers eating, temples and the view in one unhurried day. It suits anyone who flies into Mae Hong Son airport and has a day in town before moving on.

items: Morning — Sai Yud market for hot Shan food before the sky is even light
Late morning–midday — Wat Jong Kham and Wat Jong Klang on the lake, then lunch in town
Afternoon — Up to Wat Phra That Doi Kong Mu for the view over the city
Evening — Nong Jong Kham walking street for local snacks and the lit-up temples reflecting on the water

blocks.title: Before you set out
blocks.html: The loop around Nong Jong Kham is short, so comfortable walking shoes are all you need. For Doi Kong Mu, though, rent a motorbike or grab a songthaew — the road up is steep and too far to walk. Every temple here is free to enter.

blocks.text: Morning — Sai Yud market and Shan breakfast

blocks.html: Start the day the local way at Sai Yud market, the morning market in the middle of town that opens around 4am and winds down by nine. This isn't a tourist market — it's where townspeople actually buy their groceries, so the Shan food is fresh and cheap. Graze your way through and you'll be full for just a few dozen baht a plate.

items.activity: Walk into Sai Yud market in the town center
items.note: The sky is still dim and the scene is real daily life, with vendors carrying in local produce to lay out

items.activity: Try a Shan breakfast — warm winged-bean salad, khao kan jin, khanom jeen nam ngiao
items.note: Local favourites include thua nao (fermented soybean disks), gaeng hang lay, oop gai and tofu sweets, from 20–40 THB a plate

items.activity: Pick up local sweets to take along, like a-la-wa and peng mong
items.note: Shan-style desserts, good to snack on through the day

items.activity: Sit down for coffee at a café in town before the sightseeing starts
items.note: The town has several relaxed wooden-house cafés, most opening from around 8am

blocks.title: Morning market tip
blocks.html: Sai Yud wraps up early — if you arrive much past nine, stalls are already packing up. To catch everything, go before eight. Bring small cash too, since most stalls still don't take transfers.

blocks.text: Late morning — Wat Jong Kham and Jong Klang on the lake

blocks.html: Head to Nong Jong Kham, the lake at the heart of Mae Hong Son. On its bank sit two temples sharing one wall: Wat Jong Kham (on your left as you face them) and Wat Jong Klang (on the right). Both are Shan architecture, with tiered castle-style roofs trimmed in fretted zinc — the image most people picture when they think of this town.

Wat Jong Kham was built back in 1797, making it the first temple in Mae Hong Son, and its nine-tiered castle-style roof is the highlight. Next door, Wat Jong Klang holds a treasure: glass paintings by Burmese artisans depicting Jataka tales and everyday life, alongside old carved wooden figures in the temple's small museum.

items.activity: Stroll around Nong Jong Kham and photograph the temples reflecting on the water
items.note: The classic angle is from the far side, where the chedi appears upside down in the lake

items.activity: Pay your respects at Wat Jong Kham and look up at the nine-tiered roof
items.note: The town's oldest temple — free entry, dress modestly, take off your shoes before entering the hall

items.activity: See the Burmese glass paintings at Wat Jong Klang
items.note: The panels tell Jataka tales with Shan-language captions, plus antique carved wooden figures
Try khao soi, nam ngiao, or Shan dishes at a place in the old town, from 40–60 THB a plate

blocks.text: Afternoon — Doi Kong Mu and the city view

blocks.html: Wat Phra That Doi Kong Mu sits on the hill to the west of town. It's Mae Hong Son's guardian temple — locals like to call it "Kong Mu piercing the sky." Two white Shan–Burmese chedis stand here; the larger one enshrines relics brought from Mandalay, Myanmar, back in 1860. This is the spot to look out over Mae Hong Son from above, with the whole town and the airport sitting in the valley below.

items.activity: Take a ride or motorbike up Doi Kong Mu
items.note: About 3 km from town; the road is steep, so mind the bends, and you can park in the temple lot

items.activity: Pay respects at the white twin chedis
items.note: The temple is open 6:00–18:00, free entry — it's the town's guardian shrine and a popular place to make wishes

items.activity: Take in the Mae Hong Son view from the lookout
items.note: You can see the town, Nong Jong Kham and the airport runway down in the valley — a great photo spot

items.activity: Rest with a coffee or cold drink in the breeze on the hill
items.note: There's a small drinks stall at the temple, good for a break before heading back down

blocks.title: When to climb Doi Kong Mu
blocks.html: If you have the time and want the peak view, Doi Kong Mu is lovely both at dawn (in cool season a sea of mist floats over the town) and at sunset. But for this single-day plan, late afternoon with clear skies and a sharp view of the town is plenty to capture a great shot.

blocks.text: Evening — Nong Jong Kham walking street

blocks.html: Close the day at the Nong Jong Kham walking street, a small lane running about 300–400 metres along the lake, open every evening in tourist season, roughly 17:00–22:00. It starts near the post office and runs all the way to Wat Jong Kham. The stalls sell handicrafts and local food from Shan and other ethnic groups — Lisu and Karen — at easy prices.

items.activity: Walk the night market along Nong Jong Kham
items.note: Open only in tourist season (roughly Nov–Mar), daily 17:00–22:00

items.activity: Have dinner from the local street food
items.note: Shan dishes, grilled snacks and traditional sweets, just a few dozen baht a plate

items.activity: See Wat Jong Kham and Jong Klang lit up and reflected on the water
items.note: At night the chedis are floodlit and their reflection on Nong Jong Kham is the shot everyone comes back for
Woven cloth, bags, silverware and Tai gub hats — prices are slightly negotiable

blocks.html: The main plan ends at the walking street, but if you're still up for it and want to add a little more around town, there are a few stops not far away to slot in.

items.name: Wat Kam Ko
items.blurb: Another Shan temple near town, with a covered walkway and Burmese-style art, quieter than the lakeside temples.

items.name: Su Tong Pae Bridge
items.blurb: A bamboo bridge stretching across the rice fields at Ban Kung Mai Sak, about 9 km from town — good if you have a spare morning or evening.

items.name: Pang Ung / Ban Rak Thai
items.blurb: A lake and a Yunnanese Chinese village west of town. Save it for the next day if you're staying overnight.

blocks.title: Getting around
blocks.html: Everything in the old town is within walking distance except Doi Kong Mu. The easiest option is renting a motorbike by the day (around 150–250 THB/day) or chartering a songthaew. And if you fly in, Mae Hong Son airport sits right beside the town — it's under ten minutes by car to Nong Jong Kham.

faq.q: What can you do in one day in Mae Hong Son old town?
faq.a: You can fit it all into a single day: start at Sai Yud morning market for Shan food, then visit Wat Jong Kham and Jong Klang on Nong Jong Kham lake, head up to Wat Phra That Doi Kong Mu in the afternoon for the city view, and finish at the Nong Jong Kham walking street in the evening. Everything is in or near the old town, and most of it is walkable.

faq.q: Is there an entry fee for Doi Kong Mu, and what time does it open?
faq.a: Entry is free. The temple is open roughly 6:00–18:00 daily and sits about 3 kilometres from town. The road up is steep, so a motorbike or songthaew is the way to go. It's the spot for a high view over Mae Hong Son.

faq.q: What days and hours is the Mae Hong Son walking street open?
faq.a: The Nong Jong Kham walking street runs every day during tourist season (roughly November to March), around 17:00–22:00, along the edge of the lake. Expect local crafts and Shan food at easy prices.

faq.q: What time does Mae Hong Son's morning market open, and what's there to eat?
faq.a: Sai Yud market opens very early, from around 4am to nine, with traditional Shan food like warm winged-bean salad, khanom jeen nam ngiao, gaeng hang lay, oop gai, tofu sweets and local desserts. Go before eight, as stalls wind down quickly.

faq.q: When is the best time of year to visit Mae Hong Son town?
faq.a: Cool season, around November to February, when the weather is pleasant, skies are clear, and you have a chance to catch a sea of mist over the town from Doi Kong Mu in the morning. It's also when the walking street is open and the town is at its liveliest.
